title: Reporting Guidelines and Writing the Statistical Methods

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: A reporting guideline is a checklist, often with a flow diagram, that states the minimum information a report of a given study design must contain so that readers can judge its validity and reproduce it. The EQUATOR Network (“Enhancing the QUAlity and Transparency Of health Research”) collects them. The statistical methods section states, for each analysis, what was done, with what software, to which data, and why.

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html: Everything in this chapter is invisible to a reader unless you report it: how people were selected, how many were lost, how exposure was measured, which confounders were adjusted for and why. The guidelines are the lists of what reviewers and readers need. Choose the guideline by design at the protocol stage, not after the paper is written, because some items (a registered protocol, a sample size calculation, a flow diagram) cannot be produced afterwards.

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html:
Guideline by design (EQUATOR Network):

Design Guideline Notes
Randomised trial CONSORT 2025 update, “a 30-item checklist and a flow diagram” (CONSORT website); extensions for cluster and non-inferiority trials
Trial protocol SPIRIT
Observational (cohort, case-control, cross-sectional) STROBE “a checklist of 22 items” (Vandenbroucke et al., 2007)
Diagnostic accuracy STARD
Prediction model TRIPOD TRIPOD+AI (Collins et al., 2024) supersedes TRIPOD 2015 (recall §15.5.2)
Systematic review and meta-analysis PRISMA PRISMA 2020: a 27-item checklist and a flow diagram (Page et al., 2021; recall §15.7.4)
Case report CARE
Qualitative research SRQR, COREQ §17.5
Economic evaluation CHEERS

A statistical-methods paragraph template. Fill each bracket; delete what does not apply.

[Design] of [population, setting, dates]. The sample size of [n] was calculated to [estimate / detect] [quantity] with [precision / power] at α = [value], allowing [x]% non-response. Continuous variables are summarised as mean (SD) or median (IQR) according to their distribution, categorical variables as n (%). The primary outcome, [outcome], was compared between [groups] by [measure: risk ratio, mean difference …] with 95% confidence intervals. [Confounders], chosen in advance from [a causal diagram / the literature], were adjusted for by [method]. [Missing data: extent and handling]. [Sensitivity analyses]. Analyses used [software, version, packages].

Filled in for the infant cohort (recall §10.6.4 and §11.7): “Prospective cohort of 200 infants registered at two PHCs … Risk of diarrhoea was compared between infants not exclusively breastfed and exclusively breastfed infants by the risk ratio with 95% confidence interval. PHC, identified in advance as a potential confounder, was adjusted for by Mantel–Haenszel stratification; homogeneity across PHCs was assessed by Woolf’s test. The robustness of the adjusted estimate to unmeasured confounding was assessed with the E-value. Analyses used R 4.x with the epiR package.”

Table 1 conventions. Table 1 describes the participants by group (exposure groups in a cohort, arms in a trial, cases and controls in a case-control study): numbers, then each characteristic as n (%), mean (SD) or median (IQR).

Characteristic Not EBF (n = 80) EBF (n = 120)
Registered at PHC Rural, n (%) 50 (62.5) 30 (25.0)
Registered at PHC Urban, n (%) 30 (37.5) 90 (75.0)

In a randomised trial, do not add a column of p-values testing baseline differences (recall §15.9). According to the CONSORT statement such testing “should not be performed” (de Boer et al., 2015). In an observational study, the imbalance in Table 1 is information about confounding (here, PHC); describe it rather than test it.

Results: effect and interval before p. The ICMJE asks authors to “quantify findings and present them with appropriate indicators of measurement error or uncertainty (such as confidence intervals)” and to “Avoid relying solely on statistical hypothesis testing, such as P values, which fail to convey important information about effect size and precision of estimates”, and to “Specify the statistical software package(s) and versions used” (ICMJE).

  • Weak: “Not being exclusively breastfed was significantly associated with diarrhoea (p < 0.001).”
  • Better: “Diarrhoea occurred in 41.3% of infants not exclusively breastfed and 11.7% of exclusively breastfed infants (RR 3.54, 95% CI 2.02 to 6.17); after adjustment for PHC, RR 2.93 (1.60 to 5.35).”

points.html: Many of reviewers’ statistical objections are predictable; check before submission: sample size not justified; flow of participants and losses not shown; confounders chosen by significance rather than reasoning (recall §11.7); p-values without effect sizes; baseline p-values in a trial; subgroup claims without an interaction test (recall §11.7); missing data unmentioned (§15.4); multiple comparisons unaddressed (recall §8.5).
Report numbers to a precision the data support; this book gives risk ratios to two decimals and percentages to one.
Attach the completed checklist when you submit; many journals require it.
